results.evidence: External figures disagree: one route page gives about 6 mi round trip with ~2,000 ft gain (direct ridge line from the 1.4-mi saddle), a trip report via the East Peak gives 6 mi and ~2,500 ft, and an overnight report via the Watson Lakes camp gives ~8 mi and ~3,000 ft for the scramble portion. No two independent sources agree on one total for this Watson-Lakes line, so gain_ft (2,400), loss_ft (3,800) and the itinerary (3,800 gain) are left for a follow-up; loss_ft vs gain_ft convention is also a standing refused class.

One route page gives ~6 mi round trip (3 mi one way, matching dist_km 4.8 km) for the direct ridge line; another trip report also gives 6 mi; an overnight via the Watson Lakes camp gives ~8 mi round trip (~4 mi one way). None supports the 4.7-mi one-way summit waypoint or the ~9-10 mi itinerary total, and the sources describe different lines, so no value was adopted.

results.fact: Which summit is the true summit / side of approach
results.correct_value: The true summit (6,221 ft) lies WEST of a separate, lower East Peak; the route climbs from the Watson Lakes on the north side to the ~5,900 ft col between the East Peak and the western summits, then goes west along the south side of the ridge to the summit block.
results.evidence: Peak data lists Mount Watson at 6,221 ft with a separate 'Mount Watson, East Peak' 0.4 mi away; another peak list carries 'East Watson' at 6,180 ft, lower than the main summit. A route summary describes east and west summits separated by a saddle reached by a snow finger, and an overnight trip report reaches a 5,900 ft saddle via the east gully then traverses the ridge to the summit block. The beta and face fields calling the East summit the true summit were the outliers; the itinerary, bivy and approach-variant fields already agree.

results.evidence: The Watson Glacier is a real feature on the peak's north slope, and a route summary describes a snow finger (with a possible moat) leading to the saddle between the east and west summits; the overnight report describes snow travel but no glacier crossing. No source establishes whether the standard line's snow finger counts as glacier/crevassed terrain or whether parties descend onto the Watson Glacier, so the safety fields ('no glacier travel') and the beta/rack/hazard mentions of a glacier apron were left for follow-up.

results.correct_value: The descent is the north-side (Beckey-Schmidtke) rappel line on double ropes; a single rope is not enough.
results.evidence: The first-ascent party's own account records descending the standard north-face route with double-rope rappels on a 60 m and a 50 m rope (two raps near the summit, downclimbing, then three more to the snow, then downclimbing the couloir); the journal note confirms they descended the standard north-face route. Reports of that north-side line describe about ten 60 m rappels, and an encyclopedia entry says ten or more. The gear list's single 60 m rope was the outlier and was changed; the count note already presents a 4-to-10+ range (note: the account read gives five double rappels to the snow, not four to the col, so the note's first-hand figure should be re-checked).

results.evidence: The timing fields measure base-to-summit (8 h) and summit-to-base (4 h); the 17 h figure is the whole push from the shoulder camp, including the glacier approach to and from the face. The first-ascent account fits both: first pitch ~8 am, summit ~4:30 pm, back at the lower bergschrund ~9 pm, camp ~10 pm after a 3 am start.

The first-ascent party's own trip report dates the climb July 23-25, 2001, and the journal note appeared in the 2002 volume (which normally reports the previous year's climbs) without stating the year. fa and approach_variants say July 2002. Only one source names the year explicitly, so no FA change was made.

results.fact: Route identity: North Face vs East Ridge
results.correct_value: The Beckey-Schmidtke route climbs the north-face couloir and the north arête; it is not an East Ridge route.

Modern trip reports title it the NE Face (Beckey/Schmidtke). Overview, itinerary title and one rappel note were corrected.

results.evidence: The first-ascent account gives an 800 ft, 50-degree ice couloir, and an encyclopedia entry says '50-degree or greater slopes'. No source found confirms the itinerary's 50-60 degrees with a 70-degree step or max_angle 70, nor rules it out, so no change was made.

A modern trip report describes 'about ten 60m rappels' to the glacier, and an encyclopedia entry says ten or more rappels; neither gives per-rappel lengths, and the phrase is ambiguous between 60 m ropes and 60 m rappels. Nothing supports or refutes the 30 m per-station figures in rappel_detail, so no change was made.

External dates do not support the reader's internal resolution: the first ascent was July 5, and published trip reports include June 10 (2013) and July 2-4 (2009) ascents, i.e. before mid-July, while the approach-variant text notes the couloir is safer earlier. Whether the window is Jun-Aug or mid-Jul-Sep needs more sourcing, so neither was changed.
